topics.name: Lipids as signals: steroids, terpenes, and terpenoids
know: Steroids share a core of four fused rings, three six-membered and one five-membered. Cholesterol is the parent: it modulates membrane fluidity and is converted in the adrenal cortex and gonads to the steroid hormones (cortisol and aldosterone, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone), in the liver to bile acids, and in the skin, with sunlight, to vitamin D. Being lipid-soluble, steroid hormones travel on carrier proteins, cross membranes, and act on intracellular receptors that regulate transcription.

Terpenes are built from five-carbon isoprene units joined head to tail: monoterpenes (10 C, menthol, limonene), sesquiterpenes (15 C), diterpenes (20 C, including vitamin A's retinol, which the body makes by splitting the tetraterpene β-carotene), triterpenes (30 C, squalene, the precursor of cholesterol), and the polyprenyl tail of ubiquinone. Terpenoids are terpenes with added oxygen functions.

Isoprene units come from the mevalonate pathway (acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → mevalonate → isopentenyl pyrophosphate); HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis and the target of statins.
confusions: Cholesterol is not a fat (no glycerol or ester) and is essential; the problem is its transport in LDL, not the molecule itself.

topics.name: Endocrine system: glands, hormones, and neuroendocrine links
know: The endocrine system provides specific chemical control at the level of cells, tissues, and organs. An endocrine gland releases its product, a hormone, into the blood (an exocrine gland secretes into a duct); a hormone is a signalling molecule carried by blood to distant target cells that have receptors for it. Hormones are peptides and proteins (insulin, glucagon, growth hormone, pituitary hormones), amino acid derivatives (thyroid hormones, catecholamines, melatonin), or steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, sex hormones).

Major glands and products: the hypothalamus (releasing and inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary; oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone, stored and released by the posterior pituitary); the anterior pituitary (growth hormone, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH); the thyroid (T₃ and T₄ for metabolic rate; calcitonin lowers blood calcium); the parathyroids (parathyroid hormone raises calcium); the adrenal cortex (cortisol, aldosterone, androgens) and medulla (adrenaline, noradrenaline); the pancreatic islets (insulin, glucagon); the gonads (testosterone; estrogen and progesterone); the pineal gland (melatonin); and the thymus, kidney (erythropoietin, renin), heart, gut, and adipose tissue (leptin) as secondary endocrine organs.

Neuroendocrinology: the hypothalamus is the interface, turning neural input into hormone output through the hypothalamic–pituitary portal vessels and the neurosecretory cells of the posterior pituitary; the adrenal medulla is modified sympathetic nervous tissue. Tropic hormones from the pituitary control other glands in axes (hypothalamus → pituitary → thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads).
confusions: The posterior pituitary stores hormones made in the hypothalamus; the anterior pituitary makes its own, under hypothalamic releasing hormones.

topics.name: Endocrine system: mechanisms of hormone action, transport, specificity, second messengers, and feedback
know: Hormones act only on cells with matching receptors, which is what gives them specificity despite travelling everywhere in the blood. Water-soluble hormones (peptides, catecholamines) cannot cross membranes: they bind surface receptors and act through second messengers (cAMP, IP₃ and Ca²⁺, cGMP) that activate kinases and change enzyme activity within seconds to minutes; the cascade amplifies one hormone molecule into many product molecules. Lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid hormone) travel bound to plasma proteins, diffuse into cells, bind intracellular receptors, and alter transcription over hours.

Transport: hormones reach targets only through the blood supply, so delivery depends on circulation and on carrier proteins that extend a steroid's half-life; peptide hormones are cleared in minutes. The response of a target depends on receptor number (up- and down-regulation) and on the presence of other hormones (permissive, synergistic, and antagonistic effects, as with insulin and glucagon).

Control is by feedback: in negative feedback the hormone or its effect suppresses further release (thyroid hormone inhibits TSH and TRH; cortisol inhibits ACTH and CRH; calcium inhibits parathyroid hormone), stabilizing the level; in rarer positive feedback the effect amplifies release until an endpoint (oxytocin in labour, the LH surge before ovulation). The nervous system sets many loops through the hypothalamus and can override them under stress.
confusions: Second messengers are inside the cell; the hormone (first messenger) stays outside. A hormone's effect differs between tissues because the receptors and the downstream machinery differ.

topics.name: Respiratory system
know: Functions: gas exchange (O₂ in, CO₂ out), pH control through CO₂, thermoregulation and water loss through evaporation from the airways (panting in animals), and protection by filtering particles with nasal hairs and the mucus–cilia escalator that sweeps trapped material up to be swallowed. Air passes through the nose and pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles to the alveoli, tiny thin-walled sacs wrapped in capillaries whose enormous total surface area allows exchange.

Breathing: inhalation is active, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs, enlarging the chest so that intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric and air flows in; quiet exhalation is passive elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall. Surface tension in the fluid lining the alveoli would collapse them, and the pleural fluid keeps the lungs coupled to the chest; surfactant lowers the surface tension, which is why premature infants lacking it struggle to breathe.

Alveolar exchange is by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients: alveolar P_O₂ (about 100 mmHg) exceeds venous blood's (about 40), and venous P_CO₂ (about 45) exceeds alveolar (about 40); Henry's law relates the amount of each gas dissolving to its partial pressure. Breathing is regulated by the medulla and pons, driven chiefly by central chemoreceptors sensing the pH change that CO₂ produces in cerebrospinal fluid and, less, by peripheral chemoreceptors sensing low O₂; hyperventilation blows off CO₂ and raises pH (respiratory alkalosis), hypoventilation does the reverse.
confusions: The main drive to breathe is CO₂ (through pH), not low oxygen; oxygen becomes the driver only when it is very low.

topics.name: Circulatory system: heart, vessels, blood, gas transport, and clotting
know: The circulatory system carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, ions, and fluid, removes wastes, moves heat (dilating skin vessels sheds it, constricting them conserves it), and defends the body. The four-chambered heart keeps two circuits separate: the right side pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary circulation to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood through the systemic circulation. Valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic) keep flow one way; the sinoatrial node sets the rhythm. Blood pressure is reported as systolic (contraction) over diastolic (relaxation), about 120/80 mmHg.

Arteries are thick-walled and elastic and carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; arterioles have muscular walls whose constriction is the main source of peripheral resistance and controls where blood goes; capillaries are one endothelial cell thick, the site where gases, nutrients, wastes, and heat exchange by diffusion and where fluid filters out and is partly reabsorbed; venules and veins are thin-walled, low-pressure, high-volume reservoirs with valves and the help of skeletal muscle to return blood. Endothelial cells line every vessel and release factors that control vessel tone and clotting.

Blood is plasma (water, proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones) plus cells: red cells made in bone marrow under erythropoietin and destroyed after about 120 days in the spleen and liver, white cells, and platelets. Plasma volume is regulated by the kidneys through antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone. Clotting: platelets plug a damaged vessel and a cascade of plasma factors ends in thrombin converting fibrinogen to fibrin, which meshes the clot; vitamin K and calcium are needed. Oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin in red cells (hematocrit is the red-cell fraction, about 45%); hemoglobin's sigmoidal binding curve shifts right (lower affinity, more unloading) with higher CO₂, lower pH, higher temperature, and 2,3-BPG. CO₂ is carried mostly as bicarbonate (via carbonic anhydrase in red cells), some bound to hemoglobin, and a little dissolved; the heart and vessels are regulated by autonomic nerves and by hormones such as adrenaline, angiotensin II, and antidiuretic hormone.
confusions: Arteries carry blood away from the heart regardless of oxygen content: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. The Bohr shift helps active tissue: acid and CO₂ make hemoglobin release oxygen.

topics.name: Lymphatic system
know: The lymphatic system is a one-way network of blind-ended lymphatic capillaries, collecting vessels with valves, lymph nodes, and the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts that empty into the veins near the heart. Lymph is the fluid it carries, moved by skeletal muscle contraction and breathing rather than a pump.

Functions: it returns to the blood the fluid and protein that filter out of capillaries each day (about three litres), keeping tissue fluid balanced (blocked lymphatics cause swelling, lymphedema); it absorbs dietary fats as chylomicrons through the lacteals of the intestinal villi and delivers them to the blood; and it is part of the immune system: lymph nodes filter lymph and house lymphocytes and macrophages, and lymphoid organs (bone marrow, thymus, spleen, tonsils) produce and mature lymphocytes.
Because lymph flows through nodes before returning to the blood, infection and cancer cells spread along it, which is why nodes swell in infection and are examined for metastasis.
confusions: Lymph is not a separate fluid; it is interstitial fluid once it has entered a lymphatic vessel.

topics.name: Immune system: innate and adaptive immunity
know: Innate (nonspecific) immunity is present from birth and responds the same way to any invader: barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid), phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells) that engulf microbes, natural killer cells that kill infected and tumour cells, complement proteins, inflammation, fever, and interferons. Adaptive (specific) immunity is learned, targets a particular antigen, and remembers it: B lymphocytes (from bone marrow) make antibodies (humoral immunity); T lymphocytes (matured in the thymus) include helper T cells that coordinate the response and cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells (cell-mediated immunity).

Tissues: bone marrow (where all blood cells arise and B cells mature), thymus (T-cell maturation and deletion of self-reactive clones), spleen (filters blood, mounts responses to blood-borne antigens, recycles red cells), and lymph nodes (filter lymph, where antigen-presenting cells meet lymphocytes). An antigen is any molecule recognized by a receptor; an antibody is a Y-shaped immunoglobulin whose two variable arms bind one antigen with high specificity. Antigen presentation: cells display peptide fragments on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules; MHC class I on all nucleated cells shows internal peptides to cytotoxic T cells, MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells shows ingested material to helper T cells.

Clonal selection: each lymphocyte carries one receptor specificity; the antigen selects the matching clone, which proliferates into effector cells (plasma cells secrete antibody) and long-lived memory cells that make the second response faster and stronger (the basis of vaccination). Antibodies neutralize, agglutinate, opsonize for phagocytosis, and activate complement. Tolerance to self is learned by deleting or silencing self-reactive clones; when it fails, autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus) result; MHC differences also cause transplant rejection.
confusions: Helper T cells do not kill; they direct. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected body cells; antibodies act on pathogens outside cells.

topics.name: Digestive system
know: Ingestion: saliva lubricates food and begins starch digestion with amylase; the tongue and pharynx form a bolus that the oesophagus moves to the stomach by peristalsis, waves of smooth-muscle contraction that drive the whole tract. The stomach stores and churns food into chyme; its gastric juice has hydrochloric acid (pH about 2) from parietal cells, which kills microbes and unfolds proteins, pepsinogen from chief cells, activated to pepsin to begin protein digestion, and mucus and bicarbonate from the lining that protect the stomach from digesting itself; it has a fundus, body, and antrum ending at the pyloric sphincter.

The liver sits above the gut and receives nutrient-rich blood from it through the hepatic portal vein; it makes bile, regulates blood glucose (storing glycogen, releasing glucose, making it from other molecules), synthesizes plasma proteins, and detoxifies drugs and ammonia (to urea). Bile, stored and concentrated in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum, contains bile salts that emulsify fats so lipase can work and bile pigments for excretion. The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, trypsin and chymotrypsin as inactive zymogens, nucleases) and bicarbonate through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum, where the bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid.

The small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) finishes digestion with pancreatic and brush-border enzymes and absorbs nearly all nutrients and most water through villi and microvilli, which hugely expand its surface; sugars and amino acids enter the blood, fats the lymph. The large intestine (caecum, colon, rectum) absorbs water and electrolytes and houses bacteria that ferment fibre and make vitamin K; feces are stored in the rectum and expelled through the anal sphincters. Control: hormones (gastrin stimulates acid secretion; secretin triggers pancreatic bicarbonate; cholecystokinin triggers enzyme release and gall-bladder contraction and slows the stomach), and the enteric nervous system, a local network that coordinates motility and secretion with parasympathetic stimulation and sympathetic inhibition.
confusions: Most absorption happens in the small intestine, not the stomach (which absorbs little besides alcohol and some drugs). Bile emulsifies fat; it contains no enzymes.

topics.name: Excretory system: the kidney and urine formation
know: The kidneys keep the internal environment stable: they regulate blood pressure and volume (through sodium and water handling and the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system), osmolarity (osmoregulation), acid–base balance (excreting H⁺ and regenerating bicarbonate), and they remove soluble nitrogenous waste as urea along with drugs and excess ions. Each kidney has an outer cortex and inner medulla; urine collects in the renal pelvis and passes down the ureter to the bladder, where it is stored until the sphincters relax and it leaves through the urethra.

The nephron is the working unit (about a million per kidney): blood is filtered in the glomerulus, a capillary tuft inside Bowman's capsule, by pressure, so water and small solutes but not cells or proteins enter the tubule. The proximal tubule reabsorbs most of the filtrate, essentially all glucose and amino acids, most sodium, bicarbonate, and water, and secretes H⁺, drugs, and organic acids. The loop of Henle, dipping into the medulla, creates a concentration gradient as a counter-current multiplier: the descending limb lets water out, the ascending limb pumps salt out and is impermeable to water, so the medullary interstitium becomes very salty. The distal tubule fine-tunes sodium, potassium, calcium, and pH under aldosterone and parathyroid hormone; the collecting duct, running back through the salty medulla, reabsorbs water when antidiuretic hormone inserts aquaporins, concentrating the urine.

Urine formation is therefore filtration, reabsorption, and secretion; the glomerular filtration rate (about 125 mL/min, 180 L/day, nearly all reabsorbed) is held steady by autoregulation. Osmoregulation adjusts final urine from dilute (no ADH) to concentrated (high ADH); aldosterone raises sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. The bladder's smooth muscle contracts under parasympathetic control, the internal sphincter is involuntary and the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
confusions: ADH controls water reabsorption, aldosterone controls sodium; water follows sodium in the proximal tubule but needs ADH in the collecting duct. Glucose appears in urine only when filtered load exceeds the transporters' capacity (as in diabetes).

topics.name: Reproductive system: structures and hormonal control
know: Male: the testes (gonads) make sperm in the seminiferous tubules and testosterone in Leydig cells; sperm mature in the epididymis, travel through the vas deferens, and mix with fluid from the seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands to form semen, which leaves through the urethra of the penis. Female: the ovaries (gonads) release an oocyte each cycle into the uterine (fallopian) tube, where fertilization occurs; the uterus with its endometrial lining supports the embryo, the cervix opens into the vagina, and the external genitalia include the labia and clitoris. The female gonads are internal and the gametes are produced cyclically rather than continuously.

Hormonal control: gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus drives FSH and LH from the anterior pituitary. In males, LH stimulates testosterone and FSH with testosterone sustains spermatogenesis; testosterone drives male development, secondary sex characteristics, and libido, with negative feedback (and inhibin on FSH). In females, FSH grows follicles that secrete estrogen; rising estrogen triggers an LH surge that causes ovulation at mid-cycle (about day 14 of 28); the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone and estrogen that thicken the endometrium; if no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates, hormone levels fall, and the lining is shed (menstruation). Estrogen directs female sexual development.

In pregnancy, human chorionic gonadotropin from the embryo maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone and estrogen production; parturition is driven by positive feedback of oxytocin with prostaglandins; lactation depends on prolactin for milk production and oxytocin for let-down, both released through neural reflexes from suckling. Puberty, the cycle, and sexual behaviour are integrated with the nervous system through the hypothalamus.
confusions: The LH surge causes ovulation; progesterone dominates the second half of the cycle. Menstruation is caused by the fall in progesterone, not its rise.

topics.name: Muscle system and the muscle cell: types, sarcomere, contraction, control, and fatigue
know: Muscle supports and moves the body, helps return venous blood (the skeletal-muscle pump), and generates heat (shivering). Three types: skeletal (striated, multinucleate, voluntary, attached to bone), cardiac (striated, branched cells joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions, involuntary, self-exciting), and smooth (unstriated spindle cells, involuntary, in vessels and hollow organs). Skeletal fibres are slow-twitch (red: many mitochondria and myoglobin, oxidative, fatigue-resistant) or fast-twitch (white: glycolytic, powerful, fatigue quickly); cardiac and smooth muscle contract more slowly than skeletal.

A skeletal fibre is packed with myofibrils made of repeating sarcomeres: thick myosin filaments in the A band, thin actin filaments anchored at Z lines in the I band, the H zone where only myosin lies, and the M line at the centre. Sliding filament model: myosin heads bind actin, pull (power stroke, releasing ADP and Pi), release when ATP binds, and re-cock as ATP is hydrolysed, so the filaments slide and the sarcomere shortens while the filaments keep their length. Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin until calcium binds troponin and moves it aside.

Control: a motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction (motor end plate), the fibre's action potential runs along the membrane and into the T-tubules, which trigger the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release Ca²⁺; contraction ends when Ca²⁺ is pumped back. A motor neuron and its fibres form a motor unit, and force is graded by recruiting units and raising firing rate. Cardiac contraction is triggered by Ca²⁺ entering from outside plus release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is modulated, not initiated, by sympathetic (faster, stronger) and parasympathetic (slower) nerves; smooth muscle is involuntary and autonomic. Oxygen debt: during hard work muscle uses creatine phosphate and anaerobic glycolysis, accumulating lactate; the extra oxygen consumed afterward restores creatine phosphate and clears lactate, and fatigue is now thought to reflect ion shifts, phosphate build-up, and depleted glycogen more than lactate itself (older texts blame lactic acid).
confusions: ATP is needed to release myosin from actin, which is why rigor mortis sets in when ATP runs out. The H zone and I band shorten during contraction; the A band does not.

topics.name: Skeletal system: bone, cartilage, joints, and endocrine control
know: The skeleton gives rigidity and support, protects organs (skull, rib cage), anchors muscles for movement, stores calcium and phosphate, and houses the marrow that makes blood. Vertebrates have an endoskeleton of living bone that grows with the body, unlike the external exoskeleton of arthropods that must be moulted. Bones are classified as long (limbs; a shaft of compact bone around a marrow cavity with spongy bone at the ends), short, flat, and irregular.

Bone is a connective tissue whose matrix is collagen fibres hardened by calcium phosphate crystals (hydroxyapatite): collagen resists tension, mineral resists compression. Cells: osteoblasts build matrix, osteocytes maintain it from within their lacunae, and osteoclasts dissolve it; bone is continually remodelled, and it heals and strengthens in response to load. Cartilage (chondrocytes in a firm, flexible, avascular matrix) covers joint surfaces, forms the nose, ears, and intervertebral discs, and is the template for most bones in development (endochondral ossification). Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.

Joints: fibrous (skull sutures, immovable), cartilaginous (between vertebrae, slightly movable), and synovial (hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot, and others, freely movable, with a fluid-filled capsule). Endocrine control of bone and calcium: parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, kidney reabsorption, and vitamin D activation; calcitonin lowers it; vitamin D promotes intestinal absorption; growth hormone and thyroid hormone drive growth, and estrogen and testosterone close the growth plates at puberty and protect bone mass, which is why bone loss accelerates after menopause.
confusions: Osteoblasts build and osteoclasts clear; parathyroid hormone's net effect is to raise blood calcium by taking it from bone.

topics.name: Skin system
know: Skin has two layers resting on a fatty hypodermis: the epidermis, a stratified squamous epithelium whose keratinocytes are born at the base and die as they move up into a tough, water-resistant layer of keratin, with melanocytes making pigment and Langerhans cells for immunity; the dermis, connective tissue with blood vessels, nerves, hair follicles, and glands; beneath them the hypodermis, a fat layer that insulates and cushions, is strictly not part of the skin. The keratin and lipids of the outer epidermis make the skin nearly impermeable to water, which prevents dehydration (and so supports osmoregulation).

Thermoregulation: sweat glands in the dermis secrete watery sweat whose evaporation cools; arterioles in the dermis dilate to shed heat and constrict to keep it; the fat layer insulates; and erector muscles raise hairs (goosebumps), which traps air in furred animals. These responses are run by the hypothalamus through sympathetic nerves and are modified by hormones (adrenaline, thyroid hormone).

Protection: the keratinized surface, nails, calluses, and hair resist abrasion, and the intact epidermis, its acidic surface, and its immune cells block microbes; melanin absorbs ultraviolet light. Skin also makes vitamin D under sunlight and carries receptors for touch, pressure, temperature, and pain.
confusions: Sweat cools only when it evaporates; in humid air it drips off without cooling. Vasodilation of skin vessels is a heat-loss response, not a warming one.

skills.name: Knowledge of Scientific Concepts and Principles
skills.what: Do you know the concept and can you recognize it in a new setting? These questions test recall and understanding of structures, pathways, and relationships: which enzyme, which organelle, which hormone, which germ layer.
skills.example: A question might describe a cell that cannot produce ATP by oxidative phosphorylation and ask which structure is most likely defective, expecting you to recognize the inner mitochondrial membrane.

skills.name: Scientific Reasoning and Problem-solving
skills.what: Can you use the concept to work something out? These questions ask you to predict the effect of a mutation, a drug, or a hormone change, trace a pathway forward or backward, or apply a genetic rule to a pedigree.
skills.example: Given that a drug blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, a question might ask what happens to the resting membrane potential over time, expecting you to reason that it decays toward zero as the gradients run down.

skills.name: Reasoning about the Design and Execution of Research
skills.what: Do you understand how the experiment in the passage was done and what it can show? These questions ask about controls, variables, the purpose of a step, sources of error, and whether a conclusion follows.
skills.example: After a passage describing a knockout-mouse experiment, a question might ask why the researchers included wild-type littermates, expecting you to identify them as the control that shares genetic background and environment.

skills.name: Data-based and Statistical Reasoning
skills.what: Can you read the data and judge what it supports? These questions ask you to interpret a gel, a growth curve, a kinetics plot, or a table, find a trend, and decide whether a difference is meaningful.
skills.example: Given a Lineweaver–Burk plot with and without an inhibitor, a question might ask which type of inhibition the data show, expecting you to compare the intercepts.

research_methods.name: Study designs in biology
know: Controlled experiments manipulate one variable at a time with everything else held constant; in biology the comparison is often a wild-type or vehicle-treated control, a sham surgery, or an untreated culture. Genetic tools (knockouts, knockdowns, overexpression, rescue by adding the gene back) test whether a gene is necessary and sufficient for a phenotype.

Observational and epidemiological designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) show association, not cause; model organisms (E. coli, yeast, flies, worms, zebrafish, mice) trade relevance for control, and results may not transfer to humans.

research_methods.name: Variables and controls
know: Independent variable: what the researcher changes. Dependent variable: what is measured. Controlled variables: held constant. A confounding variable changes with the treatment and could explain the result. A negative control should show no effect (buffer alone, a scrambled sequence); a positive control proves the assay can detect an effect (a known activator).
Blinding and randomization apply to animals and samples as much as to people: cages, plates, and the order of measurement should be randomized and the scorer blinded.

research_methods.name: Measurement: reliability, validity, and error
know: Reliability is reproducibility (replicates agree); validity is whether the assay measures what it claims (an antibody that cross-reacts gives a reliable but invalid signal). Random error scatters measurements and shrinks with replication; systematic error shifts them all one way (a miscalibrated pipette) and does not.

Biological replicates (different animals or cultures) capture biological variation; technical replicates (the same sample measured again) capture only measurement noise, and treating them as independent inflates significance.

research_methods.name: Sampling and bias
know: Random sampling makes a sample representative; convenience samples (one strain, one sex, one age) limit generalization. Survivorship and selection bias arise when the cells, animals, or patients that remain in a study differ from those that dropped out.
Sample size sets precision: small groups give wide confidence intervals and miss real effects (low power) or produce chance 'significant' results.

research_methods.name: Correlation and causation
know: A correlation between two measurements (gene expression and tumour size, say) does not show which causes the other or whether a third factor drives both; a manipulation with a proper control is needed for cause.
A dose–response relationship, consistency across models, temporal order (cause before effect), and a known mechanism strengthen a causal argument.

research_methods.name: Descriptive statistics
know: Mean, median, and mode locate the centre; standard deviation describes spread; the standard error of the mean (SD ÷ √n) describes how precisely the mean is known and shrinks with sample size. In a normal distribution about 68% of values lie within one SD and about 95% within two.
Skewed data (cell counts, viral loads) are often log-transformed or summarized by the median.

research_methods.name: Reading figures
know: Check the axes and units, whether a scale is linear or logarithmic (bacterial growth and dilutions are usually log), what the bars show (mean or median), and what the error bars are (SD, SEM, or confidence interval). On a gel, size runs from large at the top to small at the bottom, and band intensity tracks amount.
Survival curves, dose–response curves, and kinetics plots each have standard shapes; a shift to the right on a dose–response curve means less potency, a lower plateau means less efficacy.

research_methods.name: Significance and uncertainty
know: A p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed if there were really no effect; p < 0.05 is the usual threshold for statistical significance. A 95% confidence interval that excludes zero (or a ratio of 1) is significant at that level. Type I error is a false positive, Type II a false negative; power rises with sample size and effect size.
Significance is not importance: report the effect size. Multiple comparisons inflate false positives unless corrected.

research_methods.name: Research ethics
know: Human studies need informed consent, institutional review board approval, confidentiality, and a favourable balance of benefit to risk; vulnerable groups get extra protection. Animal studies need justification, the fewest animals that give a valid answer, minimization of pain and distress, and oversight by an animal care committee.
Data must be reported as obtained, with conflicts of interest declared; genetic and biobank data raise privacy and consent issues for relatives as well as participants.

math_toolkit.name: Genetics arithmetic
know: Punnett squares give offspring ratios; for two independent genes multiply the single-gene probabilities (product rule) and add probabilities of mutually exclusive outcomes (sum rule). Hardy–Weinberg: if the recessive phenotype frequency is q², take the square root for q, then p = 1 − q and carriers are 2pq.
Recombination frequency in percent equals map distance in centimorgans for nearby genes; it cannot exceed 50%.
math_toolkit.example: If 1 in 2,500 newborns has a recessive disease, q² = 0.0004, q = 0.02, p ≈ 0.98, and the carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 0.039, about 1 in 25.

math_toolkit.name: Exponential growth and dilution
know: A doubling population follows N = N₀ × 2ⁿ after n generations; the number of generations in time t is t divided by the generation time. Serial dilutions multiply: three 1:10 dilutions give 1:1000, so a count of 50 colonies from 0.1 mL of the final dilution means 50 × 1000 × 10 = 5 × 10⁵ cells per mL of the original.
On a semi-log plot exponential growth is a straight line; the slope gives the growth rate.
math_toolkit.example: A culture with a 30-minute doubling time grows 2⁸ = 256-fold in four hours.

math_toolkit.name: Ratios, percentages, and rates
know: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Rates (filtration, flow, reaction velocity) are amounts per time; compare them by ratio. Relative values on a graph (fold change) are read against the control set to 1.
Keep units: µg to mg divides by 1,000; mL to L divides by 1,000; a 2 mM solution is 2 mmol per litre.
math_toolkit.example: If the control enzyme rate is 20 µmol/min and the treated rate is 15 µmol/min, activity fell 25%, to 0.75 of control.

math_toolkit.name: Logs and pH
know: pH = −log[H⁺]; each pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. log 2 ≈ 0.3, log 3 ≈ 0.48, log 5 ≈ 0.7. For [H⁺] = a × 10⁻ⁿ, pH = n − log a. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]), so at pH = pKa the two forms are equal, and one unit away the ratio is 10:1.
Half-lives: after n half-lives, 1/2ⁿ remains; 10% remaining is a little more than three half-lives.
math_toolkit.example: At pH 7.4 with a pKa of 6.1, log(ratio) = 1.3, so bicarbonate to carbonic acid is about 20:1.

math_toolkit.name: Reading a kinetics or binding plot
know: On a Michaelis–Menten curve, Vmax is the plateau and Km is the [S] at half of it. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km; a competitive inhibitor shares the y-intercept, a noncompetitive one shares the x-intercept.
A sigmoidal binding curve means cooperativity; a right shift means lower affinity (higher P₅₀ or Kd).
math_toolkit.example: If Vmax is 100 units and the rate at 2 mM substrate is 50 units, Km is 2 mM; at 6 mM the rate is 100 × 6/(2 + 6) = 75 units.
